# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo

## As Compiled by His Opponent

### *Being the Complete Correspondence of Hideo Kasuga, Formerly of the Ittō-ryū, to Takeshi Morimura, Fifth Dan, Spanning the Forty Years Following the 1983 All-Japan Open Kendo Championship, with Annotations and Commentary by the Recipient*

---

**Published by Morimura Takeshi**
**Privately printed, Kamakura**
**Edition of two hundred copies**
**2024**

---

## Compiler's Preface

I am dying in an ordinary way. The doctors have a name for it, and the name is long, and the length of it seems designed to obscure how common the thing itself is. I have perhaps four months. I have perhaps less. The uncertainty is, I am told, the hardest part. The doctors have not met me. They do not know what I have found hard.

I am publishing these letters without the permission of the man who wrote them, because he is likely dead, because he would not have granted permission if alive, and because I have decided, at the age of seventy-nine, that the match between us must end even if neither player moves. Perhaps especially then.

For those who do not follow the tournament circuit—and I recognize that this collection will find readers who could not distinguish a *men* strike from a *kote*, just as certain poems about the moon reach people who have never once looked up—the essential facts are these:

In September of 1983, Hideo Kasuga entered the All-Japan Open Kendo Championship as the most accomplished swordsman of his generation. He was thirty-nine years old. He had not lost a competitive match in eleven years. His style was characterized by what the commentator Fujimoto called "the patience of geology"—he moved only when the opening existed, and the opening always existed, because he could perceive gaps in an opponent's *kamae* that others could not see, the way a mason perceives the fracture line sleeping inside a stone.

I was his opponent in the final. I was twenty-eight and had won every match that year by *ippon* within the first thirty seconds. The newspapers called me Morimura the Swift. I was hungry in the way young men are hungry, which is to say I did not yet understand that hunger is not the same thing as readiness.

We faced each other. The referee called *hajime*. And for four minutes and thirty-seven seconds, nothing happened.

I have watched the tape. Everyone who cares about this correspondence has watched the tape. The tape shows two men in *bōgu* standing at engagement distance, and then it shows Hideo Kasuga lowering his shinai, stepping back, and bowing to the judges.

*Forfeit.*

No word of explanation. He left the arena, left the hotel, left Tokyo. Within a week, it was learned that he had entered a monastery in Yamagata Prefecture. Within a month, the rumors began: that he had suffered a crisis of faith in the sword; that he had experienced a revelation of Buddhist emptiness; that he had gone mad.

The first letter arrived fourteen months later, addressed to me at the dojo where I taught in Yokohama. It was written on thin paper in ink he had mixed himself, and it discussed the nature of autumn.

I wrote back. He responded. This continued for forty years.

I will refrain from explaining what these letters contain, because that is what the letters themselves are for, and because I have spent forty years failing to explain it even to myself. I will say only that Hideo Kasuga saw something in the four minutes and thirty-seven seconds we faced each other, and that what he saw was a kind of knowledge that could not be held without also holding its consequences. And I will say that I have come to believe—slowly, the way water believes in the stone it wears away—that I have always known what he saw, even as I refused to know it.

I am publishing this correspondence as my final act in a long career of the sword. Some will call it a betrayal of Hideo's privacy. I accept that. I would say only this: he wrote the letters to *me*, and I am placing them in the world because I have come to understand that the world is the only opponent large enough to absorb what lies between us.

Regarding my annotations: I have attempted to limit myself to context and clarification. I have not always succeeded. A dying man's discipline is not what it was. The reader will forgive, or the reader will not, and either way the words remain.

One final note. I have arranged the letters chronologically. This is the simplest order and therefore the one Hideo would have hated most. He would have preferred you to read them as he wrote them: as a spiral, the center of which he could never reach.

Morimura Takeshi
Kamakura, January 2024

---

## A Note on Translation

These letters were composed in Japanese. Where I have rendered them in English, I have done so with the understanding that translation is itself a kind of forfeit—the original steps back from the arena, and something else stands in its place, wearing the same armor but moving with a stranger's rhythm.

Certain terms I have left untranslated. *Bushido*. *Kamae*. *Suki*. These words exist in English only as shadows, and I prefer shadows to lies.

—T.M.

---

## Letter One

### November 1984. Written on handmade *washi*. The ink is mixed with soot from temple charcoal.

---

Morimura,

The maples here turn late. The monks say it is the altitude, but I think it is stubbornness—the trees have decided that autumn is not yet sufficient, that something more must happen before they consent to change. I have begun to sympathize with them.

I am writing to you because I dreamed of the tournament last night, which is unremarkable—I have dreamed of it often—but this time I dreamed only of the moments before. The tying of the *men* cords. The weight of the *kote* on my hands. The particular silence of an arena in which two thousand people are holding their breath. I did not dream of what followed, because what followed is not a memory so much as a country I now live in.

You are wondering why I forfeited. Everyone wonders. I have read the articles—they reach us even here, carried by novices who have not yet learned that the world outside is a letter we have stopped opening. The theories are inventive. One writer suggested I had a stroke. Another, more creative, proposed that I had achieved *mushin*—the mind of no-mind—and that in the state of perfect emptiness I simply forgot I was fighting. This is clever enough that I almost wish it were true.

I cannot tell you why I forfeited. I recognize that this makes the act of writing to you perverse—a man who cannot speak choosing to open his mouth again and again. But I have discovered something in the monastery that I never found in the dojo: that silence is not the absence of speech but a kind of speech itself, and that what matters is not whether the silence is broken but *where one stands* while it continues.

I write to you because you stood across from me, and standing across from someone is the only intimacy the sword permits.

The abbot has asked me to tend the garden. I am learning that stones are placed not where they look most beautiful but where they *create the most useful emptiness around them*. This seems important, though I cannot say why.

I hope your students are well. I hope the dojo prospers. I hope you are not angry, though I recognize you have cause.

I will write again.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *I was angry. I was so angry I kept the letter in a drawer for three months before reading it a second time. The first time, I read it as evasion. The second time, I read it as a man trying to describe a color to someone who has never seen it, and failing, and knowing he is failing, and writing anyway. I responded with four lines about the weather in Yokohama. It was, I think, the cruelest thing I have ever done. He deserved cruelty or he deserved nothing, and I could not determine which, so I gave him the cruelty and have regretted it for thirty-nine years.*

---

## Letter Four

### June 1985. The paper is thinner. The brushwork has changed—looser, as though he has been practicing calligraphy or has stopped caring about precision. I believe it is the former.

---

Morimura,

You ask about my days. I will tell you, though you asked in a way that suggested you did not truly wish to know—the way one asks a sick relative about their health, expecting and desiring only the word "better."

I wake at four. I sit *zazen* for two hours. I eat rice and pickled vegetables. I work in the garden or repair the temple buildings—there is always something crumbling, always a beam or a tile that has decided to return to the earth from which it came. I eat again. I sit again. I sleep.

Nowhere in this schedule is there a place for the sword. And yet.

I find myself standing in the garden in *chūdan-no-kamae* with a rake in my hands. I find myself reading the spaces between the stones the way I once read the spaces between an opponent's intention and his movement. The sword is gone, but the eye remains, and the eye is the part that *caused the trouble*.

I have been reading the *Hagakure*. You will laugh—every first-year student reads the *Hagakure*, it is the kind of book young men adore because it transforms their fear of death into a philosophy and thereby makes it bearable. But I am reading it now as a man who has already died once, on a gymnasium floor in Tokyo, and I find it says different things to the dead than to the living.

Tsunetomo writes: *"The Way of the Samurai is found in death."* Every student quotes this. None of them finish the passage, which continues: *"When it comes to either/or, there is only the quick choice of death."* The word *quick* is the one I cannot stop seeing. He does not say *right*. He does not say *honorable*. He says *quick*—as though the essential quality of the choice is not its virtue but its *speed*, as though to linger in the choosing is itself the defeat.

I lingered, Morimura. In those four minutes, I lingered.

I found myself in possession of a piece of knowledge, and I could not decide quickly enough what to do with it, and the not-deciding became the decision, and here I am, in a temple in the mountains, writing letters to a man who sends me reports about the weather.

You may interpret this as you wish.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *Here the correspondence begins its long circling. The reader will note that Hideo never states directly what "knowledge" he discovered, though he returns to it in nearly every subsequent letter. In my responses—which I have chosen not to include in this collection, as they are mine and I am less brave than I am old—I never asked him to clarify. The reasons for my silence are my own.*

*I will say this: I knew. Not what he knew. But that he knew something. You do not face a man like Hideo Kasuga for four minutes and thirty-seven seconds without understanding that his stillness is not empty. His stillness was the most crowded place I have ever stood.*

---

## Letter Seven

### February 1986. A winter letter. He has included a pressed leaf—from autumn, preserved. It is still in the envelope. I have left it there.

---

Morimura,

You write that you have taken on a new student, a girl of fourteen, very fast, and that she reminds you of yourself at that age. I am glad for you. I want to speak to you about what it means to see a student's *kamae* for the first time.

When a student stands before you for the first time in proper stance, there is a moment—you know the one—where you see everything. Every strength. Every fault. The way the left foot sits tells you their patience. The angle of the shinai tells you their courage. And the shoulders—the shoulders tell you what they are afraid of, because fear lives in the shoulders before it lives anywhere else.

A good teacher sees all of this and begins the long, kind work of correction. He says: *Your left heel is too high*. He says: *Relax your right hand*. He adjusts. He guides. He takes the flaw and bends it gently toward something better, and the student grows, and this is the sacred work of teaching.

But there is another kind of seeing. There is the seeing that perceives not the flaw that can be corrected but the flaw that *is structural*—the flaw that exists because of who the student is, because of the body they were born with and the mind they have built, the flaw that cannot be removed without removing the person. This kind of seeing is a curse. It is the sword-eye turned inward, or rather turned on another with surgical precision, and what it finds is the place where a life can be undone.

I am speaking abstractly. I know this. I am always speaking abstractly, and you are always patient with it, and your patience may be the most generous thing anyone has ever given me and also the most terrible, because it allows me to continue circling without landing, and I am not certain that landing would not be better, even if the landing killed me.

Teach your student well. See her faults with the teacher's eye—the kind one. Leave the other eye closed.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *On the evening I received this letter, I went to the dojo after all the students had gone home. I stood in chūdan-no-kamae before the mirror for forty minutes. I looked at my shoulders. I looked at my left foot. I looked at the angle of my shinai.*

*I could not see what he saw.*

*This is the heart of it: I could never see what he saw, and because I could not see it, I could not know whether it was real or imagined, whether his exile was sacrifice or delusion, whether the forty years were a gift or a waste. And I could not ask, because to ask would be to admit that I suspected, and to admit that I suspected would be to change the shape of what lay between us, and what lay between us was the only shape either of us had.*

---

## Letter Twelve

### September 1988. Five years since the tournament. The brushwork has become very refined—he has clearly been studying calligraphy seriously. This is the first letter in which he mentions the concept of *suki* directly.

---

Morimura,

It is the anniversary. I suppose you know this. I suppose you mark it as I do, or perhaps you do not, perhaps for you it is a day like any other, a square on the calendar no different from the squares on either side. I cannot tell. Your letters are kind and empty, like well-built rooms in which no one lives.

I have been thinking about *suki*.

The word is translated as "opening" or "gap," and this is correct as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough. *Suki* is not merely the absence of defense. It is the *presence* of an invitation—an invitation the defender does not know he has issued, written in the language of the body, legible only to the one who stands across.

In training, we learn to perceive *suki* as opportunity. The opponent's concentration wavers; the sword-tip drifts three millimeters to the left; the weight shifts almost imperceptibly to the rear foot—and we strike. This is correct. This is the art. The *suki* opens like a door, and we walk through it, and the match ends, and everyone bows, and we have proved something about speed and perception that is satisfying in the way that solving a mathematical proof is satisfying.

But what happens when the *suki* does not open and close? What happens when it is *permanent*?
